background_and_links.details: I read the full assigned section, then its named B.1–B.4 prerequisites and 19.1, including the beginnings of those sources before their first section. B.1 explains a request is data rather than execution; B.2 separates parse and validate and defines allowlist; B.3 explains returning an actual result; B.4 distinguishes completion, limits, and errors. 19.1 supplies DIRECT, ASK, TOOL, EOS, action_correct, and joint. I additionally followed B.1’s explicit 7.11 dialogue-SFT link because SFT was unfamiliar. Other linked material was not necessary for this lesson’s local mechanism. I did not open evidence datasets, earlier reviews, or unassigned whole chapters. The two open vocabulary notes are recorded as nonblocking.

terminology.details: TOOL marks a program request, calculator is the allowed tool name, and 1+2 supplies the ordered addends. parse_action reads the structure; calculator_runtime decides whether it is allowed/available and returns a result or error. trace/raw/eos are explained as a hand-written record, not actual generation evidence. EOS is the model’s ending ID; its presence does not prove a correct answer. action_trace, runtime, and final_trace name the first model output, actual execution, and second model output. action_correct includes the full first string and EOS; end-to-end correctness also requires a correct final answer. The B background explains number families by keeping swapped numbers together, so the fixed-template caveat is understandable. The phrase 新增模態 is understandable here as adding image/audio inputs from 19.1 and the following 圖音 sentence. byte and DPO remain minor undefined labels as recorded above.

examples.details: The opening classmate example explains two different opportunities to make a mistake. For a requested 2+1, writing 1+2 preserves the mathematical sum 3 but violates the ordered-parameter rule; thus action scoring is protocol compliance as well as arithmetic. The SFT table reports 10 complete calculation requests at each stage, 10 unavailable situations, and 5 separate result-only questions; the last 5 are not additional complete loops. The cited final joint check reports 12/12 correct requests and successful executions but only 10/12 correct final responses, with both failed response strings ending normally. It separately reports 12/12 unavailable situations and 5/6 result-only questions. The held-out 1+2 and 2+1 both end at 3. I understand these as the prose’s earlier experiments, not runs I reproduced. No formal equation is introduced; plus signs are ordinary addition and fractions denote passed cases over that row’s own denominator.

program_explanation.details: The input trace is a Python dictionary with raw=TOOL:calculator:1+2 and eos=True, both manually supplied. parse_action converts this to status tool, name calculator, and integer a=1,b=2; a and b are the first and second addends. The for loop calls the same runtime twice with availability True then False. My bounded CPU execution printed {status: ok, result: 3} with 3 stored as a string when enabled, and {status: error, reason: calculator_unavailable} when disabled. The final print correctly marks the absence of any model readback or final model answer. The later run_assistant prose explains the missing step by quoting the new user input with the original question and real calculator result, which is sufficient to follow the mechanism without seeing its implementation.

exercise.details: I saved a prediction before running the exercise: change only raw from TOOL:calculator:1+2 to TOOL:unknown:1+2, leaving the import, parser, runtime, availability loop, and numbers unchanged. I predicted it would still parse as a tool action and would not be permitted to execute. The CPU output confirmed a parsed name unknown with a=1,b=2; availability True returned tool_not_allowlisted, and availability False returned calculator_unavailable. My prediction did not specify the error spelling and broadly attributed rejection to the unknown name; the actual disabled branch reports unavailability instead. Both outputs are errors rather than calculation results, so the intended difference between readable syntax and execution permission is checkable. Explicitly mentioning both loop outcomes would make the exercise’s expected output slightly easier to match, but this is not a blocker.

own_explanation.problem: An assistant may request wrong inputs or misread a correct tool result. Evaluate the full sequence rather than substituting the program result for the assistant’s final answer.
own_explanation.code_and_symbols: The code is a hand-written request example, not a trained model demonstration. raw is the compact request text; eos=True is a manual claim of a normal end; action is the parser output; available is a Boolean runtime switch; result is a returned dictionary. a=1 and b=2 are parsed integer addends, while result=3 is a string in the success dictionary.
own_explanation.numbers: SFT: 10/10 requests pass each whole-loop gate and 5/5 separate readback questions pass. Final joint: 12 requests execute correctly, 10 final answers are correct, 12 disabled-tool situations are handled, and 5 of 6 isolated readback answers are correct. 0+1 and 1+0 both have true result 1 yet distinct wrong final strings. These denominators measure different gates/groups and must not be summed.
own_explanation.exercise_prediction_and_check: Parsing unknown should succeed as structure, but execution should not produce an arithmetic success. The enabled case specifically rejects the allowlist violation; the disabled case preserves its unavailable error. This observation is saved separately from my prior prediction.
